💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other consumers.
  • Recent findings suggest that those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other consumers.

Recent findings suggest that those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

It has been revealed that don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

Industry observers note that we expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

Industry observers note that as trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail consumers. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

Sources indicate that this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

It has been revealed that if you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

Industry observers note that in a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

In a recent development, so, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other consumers and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

Recent findings suggest that if running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you blueprint to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#9032. How a 20-Year-Old Texas Climber Lost His Life on the Matterhorn

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2363 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How a 20-Year-Old Texas Climber Lost His Life on the Matterhorn

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kieran Liner, a 20-year-old climber based in Austin, TX, died in an accident on the Matterhorn in October.
  • A 20-year-old climber named Kieran Liner from Austin, Texas, died on October 27 after falling from the Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge.
  • It has been revealed that valais Cantonal Police said the two climbers were ascending shortly after 6 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kieran Liner, a 20-year-old climber based in Austin, TX, died in an accident on the Matterhorn in October. (Photo: Courtesy Precenia Newman).

A 20-year-old climber named Kieran Liner from Austin, Texas, died on October 27 after falling from the Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge. He was climbing with his friend Eli Hawkins.

It has been revealed that valais Cantonal Police said the two climbers were ascending shortly after 6 a.m. when rocks fell near them at about 11,500 feet. Hawkins lost sight of Liner and immediately called for help. An Air Zermatt helicopter responded. Rescuers found Liner below the route and pronounced him dead at the scene.

Prosecutors opened an investigation to determine the precise circumstances of the fall. The initial police statement reported rockfall nearby, but didn’t specify exactly how Liner fell or died.

Hawkins, who claims he met Liner in Austin around five years ago, called him his “best bud” and his climbing partner. “It is what it is,” Hawkins told Climbing. “He died doing what he loved.”.

Sources indicate that originally from Pensacola, Florida, Liner had lived in Austin since 2020. According to Hawkins, Liner liked Modest Mouse, IPAs, and American Spirit Blues. But what he loved most, Hawkins wrote, was climbing in the mountains.

Sources indicate that in an obituary shared last week, Liner’s sister Precenia Newman remembered her younger brother as a skateboarder, golfer, and alpinist—someone who brought the same enthusiasm to everything he pursued. “He approached everything in life with 150% of himself,” Newman wrote.

It has been revealed that newman described a close circle of friends who had become family through shared adventures and everyday life. Among them was Hawkins, whose friendship and life as Liner’s roommate she singled out as especially meaningful. She also remembered the love surrounding Liner from his parents, Justine Hamel and Nick Liner, as well as his siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews. Newman has organized a fundraiser to bring him home so the family can celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin.

While Hawkins grew up climbing as a kid with his father and uncle, Liner got into the sport later in life, but it promptly became his passion. Hawkins noted the two of them had strong mentors, including Hawkins’s dad Stephen, Ben Darce, and his uncle Bryan Hawkins who owns a climbing gym in Everett, Washington. “He was fearless,” Hawkins said of Liner. “I was fearless—still am. I’m going to keep climbing for him. We just climbed hard and partied hard.”.

According to recent reports, this past July, Liner had started an Instagram account called @mountkieran dedicated primarily to climbing and mountaineering content. His first reel captured climbing Mt. Rainier. Most of his content leaned humorous, with jokes about “Conrad Anger” and poking fun at himself as an “Austin influencer” while board climbing.

But occasionally, Liner shared more serious content, like footage of ascending a steep snow pitch with a quote from Reinhold Messner: “To go on an adventure, you need difficulties, you need danger. If death were not a possibility, coming out would be nothing.”.

Generally considered the most popular and easiest route by which to ascend the Matterhorn, the Hörnli Ridge rises roughly 4,000 vertical feet from the Hörnli Hut to the 14,692-foot summit. Rated AD (“fairly difficult”) on the alpine scale, the route combines sustained exposed scrambling with technical rock climbing rated around 5.4. In general, parties take four to five hours for the ascent, plus another five to six hours for the descent, which involves downclimbing and rappelling much of the same terrain.

Fixed ropes assist climbers on certain sections, but parties also bring their own ropes. Snow and ice can be encountered near the summit, requiring crampons and an ice axe. The technical grade captures only part of the challenge of navigating and descending that exposed terrain in mountaineering boots.

To learn more about the Hörnli Ridge where Liner’s accident took place, I reached out to my friend Steph Abegg, who claimed the fastest known time by a woman on the route this past summer.

In 1985, Abegg’s dad soloed the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Twenty years later, when Abegg and her sister were in Zermatt and decided to climb it, that was the image they held in their minds. Their dad was an experienced climber, and he’d enjoyed ideal conditions on his ascent.

Accordingly, the Abegg sisters expected a casual adventure. Instead, they encountered verglas—a thin glaze of ice on the rock—and a whiteout. They turned around at the Solvay Hut, an emergency shelter at 13,133 feet. At this point, they were roughly 2,440 vertical feet above the Hörnli Hut, where the climb begins, and still about 1,560 feet below the summit.

“It could be said I underestimated the Matterhorn myself in 2005,” Abegg told me. “Had we continued, it’s entirely possible we could have gotten into trouble.”.

This past summer, Abegg returned, climbing the Hörnli Ridge with a partner before completing a solo, unsupported round trip from Zermatt in 10 hours, 8 minutes, and 19 seconds—the fastest women’s time then recorded on the FKT website, supported or unsupported. A month later, Kalie McCrystal lowered the record to 6 hours, 47 minutes, and 33 seconds.

According to recent reports, the route’s moderate technical grade, fixed ropes, and popularity can make the Hörnli Ridge seem approachable. But finding the line and staying on solid rock demands attention. Stray from the standard route and the rock can become looser. Altitude, changing weather, and fall consequences add to the difficulty.

In a recent development, during Abegg’s partnered ascent this past summer, a washing-machine-sized boulder was accidentally dislodged. It tumbled down a gully, triggering what she described as a significant rockslide, mostly off route. Higher up, loose rock littered the climbing line. Abegg described rocks ranging in size from marbles to baseballs, or even volleyballs, that climbers could knock onto people below. The terrain, she mentioned, had historically remained under snow year-round.

According to recent reports, “Had to move very carefully,” she wrote. Guides stopped taking clients up the route during her trip.

Aside from the omnipresent risk of rockfall in any alpine environment, a 2025 study found that climate change has caused an increase in rockfall on the Matterhorn as permafrost thaws. Just a couple months ago, German online magazine Lacrux published an article about the increasing hazards of rockfall on the Matterhorn, as well as on Mont Blanc.

“Having the innate mountain sense to know when to call it is a valuable quality on an objective like this,” Abegg mentioned.

Andy Hansen, an IFMGA-certified (International Federation of Mountain Guides) guide based in Longmont, Colorado, has guided clients on the Matterhorn twice. Speaking from his own experience, he strongly recommends hiring a guide for a first attempt.

He remarked recreational climbers in Western Europe are generally more accustomed to hiring guides than their counterparts in the United States. One advantage of hiring a guide on the Hörnli Ridge is how closely they follow variable conditions on a route, according to Hansen.

“The local guides have an intimacy with the mountain that gives them the advantage of having the route finding dialed, understanding the conditions of the mountain from day to day, and knowing where and when to move swiftly to manage the rockfall hazard,” Hansen told me.

In a recent development, hansen observed an unusual amount of rockfall in the Alps this past spring and summer, calling the Hörnli Ridge noticeably more unstable. He pointed to local guides’ familiarity with the ridge and their day-to-day knowledge of its conditions. A weather forecast can tell any climber how warm it’s likely to get, but knowing the ridge helps a guide judge which sections are most prone to rockfall, where to move quickly to limit exposure, and whether to climb that day at all.

However, whether a guide would have changed the outcome for Liner is an entirely different question. “It’s virtually impossible to say with any degree of certainty that had this party been with a mountain guide, the outcome would have been any different,” Hansen remarked. In his view, it was the kind of misfortune that could befall a guided party, too.

Hawkins told Climbing that they were aware of the risk of rockfall and had accepted it as a possible and uncontrollable hazard that you can’t “really do anything about.” He added that he never considered hiring a guide because he has sufficient experience and wants to take on alpine objectives independently. “If you do hire a guide, you didn’t climb the mountain,” he said of his philosophy.

According to recent reports, while a guide is not required to climb the Matterhorn, it does materially improve your chances of reaching the summit. According to Global Summit Guide, an independent, research-based mountaineering resource based in Utah, the summit rate varies considerably depending on whether climbers are traveling with a guide.

Industry observers note that A Global Summit Guide report updated this past July states that while the overall Matterhorn success rate is 55%, guided climbers see a 72% success rate, while unguided climbers hover around a 38% success rate. Meanwhile, first-timers like Liner and Hawkins only have an 18% shot at reaching the top. Furthermore, during the popular climbing season of May through October, October has the lowest success rate of 22%.

Industry observers note that global Summit Guide also reinforces the Matterhorn’s reputation as Europe’s most deadly mountain, with an average of eight to 12 fatalities annually. They note that about 1 in 140 climbers perish in their attempt to summit. More than 500 people (and counting) have died on the Matterhorn to date.

Dialogue and debate over the broader trends indirectly related to Liner’s death have already  emerged in the climbing community.

In a recent development, after Liner died, a Reddit thread in r/Mountaineering sparked debate about the climbing-related content he and Hawkins had posted on their Instagram accounts. “Obviously, there are videos of me and him partying in Europe, but when we’re actually climbing, I take precautions and I’m not an idiot when I climb,” Hawkins told Climbing. “I take safety as a number one precaution.” He added that Liner would “probably be laughing” at what Hawkins sees as misinformed comments online.

It has been revealed that then, in an Instagram reel posted on November 2, Washington-based gear manufacturer High Mountain Gear turned the discussion toward a different topic: a video Norwegian climber Magnus Midtbø made about his 2025 Matterhorn solo. High Mountain Gear took particular glitch with Midtbø looking up how to use crampons shortly before his climb. In the comments of High Mountain Gear’s reel, some agreed that a climber with Midtbø’s reach ought to think about the example he sets. Others asked why he was being brought into a conversation about someone else’s accident.

Hawkins explained that he and Liner had set the Matterhorn as a massive goal independent of any online content. “It’s just a climb we wanted to do for a long time,” Hawkins noted of the Matterhorn. “It had nothing to do with any Instagram videos.” He noted that he wasn’t very familiar with Midtbø’s Matterhorn video.

Beyond this recent incident, when Midtbø’s video came out, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported that Midtbø talked openly about his limited preparation. He struggled with the altitude and got off route. Other climbers had to call him back to the right line. Once he got down, he admitted he had underestimated the risk and urged viewers against following his example. Air Zermatt’s rescue chief Anjan Truffer told SRF that he worried viewers might still interpret Midtbø’s climb as a success, without appreciating the gap between his climbing ability and their own.

In Midtbø’s defense, however, he could have cut the moments when he was tired, lost, or scared. But he chose to leave them in. Some viewers in the YouTube comments took the climb as a cautionary tale. Others wanted a follow-up with a guide explaining where things nearly went wrong. Ultimately, given the irrelevance of Midtbø’s video to Hawkins’s and Liner’s Matterhorn objective, as well as the full disclosures that Midtbø provided in his video, the notion that YouTube content is to blame for this or any other fatality seems besides the point.

As a guide, Hansen sees responsibility on both sides of the screen. He stated creators like Midtbø have some accountability for what they put out, even when they include a disclaimer. But viewers must assess whether their own skills match the demands of any climb described in online content.

Abegg’s father came home with a story about soloing the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Abegg and her sister came home with a story about turning around at the Solvay Hut. Midtbø came home, too. But in his video, you can see how close he came to a different outcome when he lost the route on exposed terrain.

Sources indicate that kieran Liner didn’t come home. He was 20 years old. The mountain doesn’t care what drew you there, whose story you heard, or how long you spent preparing. Even the most experienced climber can be in the wrong place at the wrong time, especially when it comes to escalating hazards like rockfall.

In a recent development, liner’s family is planning to celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin. In her obituary, Newman invited everyone who knew him, shared his adventures, or found inspiration in his life to join them. “Whether you knew him for a lifetime or crossed paths with him only briefly,” she wrote, “you are part of the story he leaves behind.”.

Climbing Magazine reached out to Kyle Willis of High Mountain Gear and Magnus Midtbø for comment, but have not received a response.

#9030. Do Skiers Really Need Another Outerwear Brand? Atomic Thinks So.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1539 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

Do Skiers Really Need Another Outerwear Brand? Atomic Thinks So.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Atomic's outerwear features clean lines, minimal logos, and ski-specific details, including articulated construction designed to allow freedom of movement.
  • Industry observers note that the ski world probably doesn’t need another outerwear brand.
  • So when Atomic, the Austrian brand best known for its skis, boots, and bindings, revealed it was getting into apparel, I had a pretty obvious question: Why?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Atomic's outerwear features clean lines, minimal logos, and ski-specific details, including articulated construction designed to allow freedom of movement. (Photo: Cam McLeod/Atomic).

Industry observers note that the ski world probably doesn’t need another outerwear brand. Dozens of other companies already make quality ski jackets and pants; we’re not exactly short on options.

So when Atomic, the Austrian brand best known for its skis, boots, and bindings, revealed it was getting into apparel, I had a pretty obvious question: Why?

Apparently, Atomic had the same thought.

According to recent reports, at a recent North American launch event I attended at Sundance Mountain Resort in Utah, Atomic acknowledged the challenge of entering an already crowded market. But their answer was simple: After more than 70 years developing ski equipment, who better to make clothing for skiers than a tech giant that lives and breathes skiing?

Sources indicate that fair enough. Though plenty of established apparel companies could make the same argument.

In a recent development, after handling and trying on several pieces from the new collection, including some Gore-Tex Pro outerwear coming next year, I came away impressed. The clothing has clean lines, thoughtful colors, familiar technical materials, and small design details that suggest someone actually thought about what it’s like to spend a day skiing in this stuff.

In a recent development, I haven’t skied in it yet, so the real performance test is still to come. But there’s enough here to make Atomic’s latest expansion worth a closer look. It is a significant expansion, including a complete skiwear collection, from insulated resort jackets and technical shells to bibs, midlayers, base layers, and lifestyle pieces.

Of course, Atomic isn’t the first ski equipment tech giant to see an opportunity in apparel. Salomon, Armada, and Rossignol have all made the move, while Black Diamond, whose roots are in climbing and backcountry skiing, did the same more than a decade ago. Atomic itself has steadily expanded beyond skis, boots, and bindings over the years, adding helmets and goggles to its lineup.

Recent findings suggest that so the move into apparel isn’t entirely surprising. But what does Atomic bring to an already crowded category?

For starters, Atomic isn’t entering the apparel business entirely on its own. The company is part of Amer Sports, which also owns Salomon and Arc’teryx, two brands with decades of experience making technical outerwear. Atomic’s designers explained that they’ve been able to draw on existing fabric research, development resources, and manufacturing expertise within the group.

In a recent development, atomic also brings its own experience developing ski equipment since 1955. I’ve visited the firm’s headquarters in Altenmarkt, Austria and seen firsthand how its engineers develop skis, boots, and bindings, taking prototypes from the office to the snow in minutes and bringing that feedback back into development. Now, outerwear designers follow a similar process, with access to on-snow testing close to headquarters.

According to recent reports, then there’s Atomic’s reputation. In SKI’s 2026 ski test results, Atomic was among the top three most-recognized brands, earning distinctions in categories ranging from backcountry and powder to frontside carving. In my view, that’s a track record worth protecting, and one that gives skiers a reason to take their clothing seriously.

The materials are reassuringly familiar, too. Atomic uses established insulation and fabric technologies from PrimaLoft and Pertex, alongside its own waterproof fabrics. Gore-Tex Pro will join the collection in fall 2027.

Industry observers note that for the current lineup, the differences are fairly straightforward. The Revent 2L Insulated Jacket and Pants use Atomic’s 2LAYR Move, a two-layer fabric rated at 20,000 mm waterproofing, with PrimaLoft Silver synthetic insulation for warmth. They’re designed for skiers who prefer an insulated jacket and pants rather than managing multiple layers.

It has been revealed that the Revent 3L Jacket and Bib Pants, meanwhile, use Atomic’s 3LAYR Protect, a three-layer fabric also rated at 20,000 mm waterproofing. They’re uninsulated shells, giving skiers more flexibility to add or remove layers as temperatures and conditions change.

Of course, familiar materials and impressive specifications are only a starting point. How a jacket is cut, how the seams are constructed, and how everything fits and moves together can make the difference between loving your gear and being annoyed by it before lunchtime.

And that’s where some of Atomic’s smaller design choices caught my attention.

Atomic describes its approach as performance-first rather than fashion-first, and some of the most interesting details are the ones you might not notice until you’re actually wearing the clothing.

According to recent reports, the women’s Snowcloud Puff Jacket is a good example. It has a slightly cropped silhouette, an insulated powder skirt, and a removable hood.

Recent findings suggest that take the hood off, and there aren’t exposed snaps or awkward attachment points that make it look like something is missing. It’s still a finished-looking jacket.

That matters when you’re using a puffy in different ways. A hood is nice around town or when the jacket is your outermost layer on a dry day. But under a shell that already has a hood, it can feel bulky and unnecessary.

Recent findings suggest that the Revent 2L Shell Anorak, a relaxed, unisex shell, also caught my eye. It has the oversized silhouette and kangaroo pocket you’d expect, but the concealed chest pocket inside the collar was an added touch you don’t often find in anorak styles. As someone who finds it incredibly annoying to put a phone or sunglasses in a kangaroo pocket and have everything bouncing around, I appreciated that.

Other ski-specific details include lift-pass pockets on the left sleeves of most jackets (not just outer shells), helmet-compatible hoods, well-placed ventilation, reinforced pant cuffs, and articulated construction, including pre-shaped elbows and knees designed to accommodate how skiers actually move.

Industry observers note that none of these features is revolutionary, of course. But they’re familiar details, executed with the kind of practical attention that matters when you’re spending a full day in ski gear.

As for fit, the pieces I tried generally ran true to size, with a slightly longer, freeride-inspired cut that felt relaxed without being baggy. That stated, at six feet tall, I found both pairs of softshell and hardshell pants a little shorter than I’d like.

It has been revealed that atomic’s 2026–’27 apparel collection is available now at Atomic.com. Looking ahead to fall 2027, skiers can expect to find Atomic apparel at select retailers and ski shops as well.

Atomic clearly understands that skiers care about style, too. The aesthetic is clean and understated without being boring. Muted but thoughtful colors, cropped puffies, relaxed anoraks, and monochromatic outfits give the collection plenty of visual appeal. The silhouettes and design details are consistent across categories, so the pieces look like they belong together without requiring a fully matching kit.

But one of my favorite design details is something you might never notice unless you’re a skier, like me, who rolls up your pant cuffs when you’re out of your boots.

According to recent reports, on the inside of the right pant cuff, Atomic has hidden its name. That’s the only time the wordmark appears, which feels decidedly cool.

Industry observers note that it’s also a pretty good introduction to Atomic’s approach to branding. You won’t find its name prominently displayed across the collection. Instead, the Atomic star appears subtly printed on sleeves or worked into seam placements and color blocking.

The design is recognizable once you know what to look for, but it doesn’t announce itself from across the lift line.

In a recent development, like Wild Rye and a handful of other ski apparel brands of late, Atomic seems comfortable letting the design speak for itself. There’s something confident about that, especially in a sport where logos can be as loud as the colors they’re printed on.

It has been revealed that after all, is there a better compliment than someone saying, “That’s a sick jacket. Who makes it?”.

With skis, boots, bindings, helmets, goggles, and now clothing, Atomic can outfit skiers almost completely under one brand.

That doesn’t mean there’s any reason to buy everything from Atomic. Most of us mix and match equipment, developing relationships with different brands for different reasons. Maybe you love your Atomic skis but swear by another company’s boots. Your favorite jacket might come from a brand that doesn’t make hardgoods, and your base layers from somewhere else entirely.

Still, there’s something to be said for gear designed to work together.

Think about wearing a helmet and goggles from the same company. When the fit is seamless, it’s one less thing to worry about.

Recent findings suggest that atomic seems to be taking a similar approach to its apparel, developing shells, insulation, and base layers with complementary fits, colors, and layering systems. Whether that delivers a meaningful performance advantage remains to be seen, but I understand the intent.

According to recent reports, ultimately, that’s the appeal of well-designed ski equipment, regardless of whose name is on it. We spend enough time and money figuring out what to wear and what to ski. Once we’re on the mountain, we shouldn’t have to think about any of it.

The gear does its job. We get to ski.

#9029. Tech Report: The Feds Want to Sell Off Public Land and Overhaul the National Park Service

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1129 w)

Tech Report: The Feds Want to Sell Off Public Land and Overhaul the National Park Service

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NPS policies could be slated to change (Photo: Smith Collection/Gado / Getty Images).
  • Sources indicate that with Democrats slated take control the House of Representatives and Senate on January 3, the Trump Administration is advancing multiple policies that could impact U.S.
  • According to recent reports, among the proposals are a sweeping selloff of territory controlled by the Interior Department, the limiting of public input on decisions made by the Bureau of Land Management, and a dramatic restructuring of the National Park Service (NPS), among others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NPS policies could be slated to change (Photo: Smith Collection/Gado / Getty Images).

Sources indicate that with Democrats slated take control the House of Representatives and Senate on January 3, the Trump Administration is advancing multiple policies that could impact U.S. national parks and other public lands.

According to recent reports, among the proposals are a sweeping selloff of territory controlled by the Interior Department, the limiting of public input on decisions made by the Bureau of Land Management, and a dramatic restructuring of the National Park Service (NPS), among others. The intends have sparked strong criticism from nonprofits, conservation groups, and lawmakers.

Recent findings suggest that “It feels like they’re trying to rush this stuff through in the dark of night,” Edward Stierli, vice president of government affairs for the National Parks Conservation Association, told Outside. “We know they’re trying to move on these reorganizations before the end of the year because they know in 2027 there will be a higher level of accountability.”.

Here’s a look at some of the controversial public lands policies that the administration is considering.

On November 7, The Washington Post published a report stating that the Department of Interior (DOI) was planning a dramatic restructuring of both the National Park Service and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Citing internal DOI documents, the WaPo stated that DOI officials are considering “pending duty station changes” to the locations where NPS staff work. Outside reached out to the DOI for comment but did not hear back prior to the publishing of this story.

In a recent development, the report comes two months after the Washington Sun reported that the DOI was considering realigning its 433 NPS units under a so-called hub-and-spoke management model. Currently, all 433 NPS units retain some autonomy in making their own decisions.

Under the proposed model, decision-making power would be centralized at larger parks, while smaller “spoke” park units would lose some power.

Stierli told Outside that there’s already regional hub-and-spoke models around resource sharing in the NPS that are effective. But moving to a sweeping hub-and-spoke management model would likely lead to the loss of staff and expertise at smaller sites.

“When you go to Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania the tour you get there is incredible; it makes everyone cry, because it was designed by someone who is steeped in the history there,” Stireli mentioned. “If you were to move that position to a different park, or to a variety of different parks, you’re not going to get the same level of expertise.”.

Recent findings suggest that even if the hub-and-spoke model doesn’t move forward, other plans are afoot for the agency. In its new strategic plan for 2026 to 2030, the DOI highlighted a move to “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” The agency has already been crippled by consolidation: in 2025, the NPS lost nearly a quarter of its full-time staff to buyouts and layoffs.

Recent findings suggest that on November 11, the DOI published a sweeping strategic strategy for 2026 through 2030 that outlines the department’s large-scale path for managing the 11 agencies under its control, including the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

In his opening letter DOI secretary Douglas Burgum said the agency’s primary focus was to make public lands available for the country’s goals around energy production and industry.

The document also stated that the DOI would “work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities, and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands.”.

“Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” the plan states.

The proposal to sell public lands drew sharp objections from critics.

“Secretary Burgum’s initiative threatens the lands where families hike, camp, hunt, and fish, the wildlife habitats that sustain our ecosystems, and the natural, cultural, and historic treasures we have a responsibility to protect for future generations,” Loren Blackford, executive director of the Sierra Club, mentioned in a statement. “The administration should be investing in protecting our public lands and the people who steward them, not looking for ways to shrink and block public access to them.”.

This is the Trump Administration’s second attempt at a sweeping sale of public lands. In June 2025, Utah Senator Mike Lee spearheaded a initiative to sell 3 million acres of land managed by the Bureau of Land Management and U.S. Forest Service. The plan was ultimately torpedoed amid mounting bipartisan opposition.

On November 10, the Bureau of Land Management published a proposal titled Revision of Regulations for Planning, Programming, Budgeting that includes a series of foundational changes to the way the agency proceeds with public land decisions. The BLM manages 245 million acres of public land, more than any agency.

At the top of the list would be limiting the public’s ability to comment on the BLM’s plans for parcels of public lands, and eliminating the agency’s need to produce a document called an Environmental Impact Statement, which outlines how the move will impact the local flora and fauna, prior to a change.

Right now, the public gets 90 days to comment on major changes to the way the BLM manages land. The proposal would shrink this to 30 days, or replace a comments period with public meetings in some situations.

Steve Pearce, the director of the BLM, said the changes would streamline the BLM’s process for approving new projects.

“The current planning process is too slow, too complicated and weighed down by outdated requirements,” Pearce said in a statement. “These proposed changes would help the BLM make decisions more efficiently, reduce costs for taxpayers and improve coordination with the people and communities that rely on public lands.”.

But critics argue that the 90-day public comments period is an imperative.

“Gutting transparency, review, and public engagement requirements within the West’s most ecologically sensitive wildlife corridors, watersheds, and cultural resources are the actions of cowards trying to fast-track industrial development at any and all social costs,” said Kara Matsumoto, senior policy director at the Conservation Lands Foundation, in a release.

Advocates in Texas are awaiting the return of bulldozers and trucks to Significant Bend National Park, where the construction of a barrier along the U.S.-Mexico border has been on hold since September.

On November 9, the U.S. Supreme Court voted to allow the construction to continue, overriding the decision of a federal judge who had ordered it to stop. In October, the Trump Administration filed papers to challenge the order and fast-track the case to the Supreme Court. With the approval, the administration is likely to continue a project that’s been criticized by locals, Texas law enforcement, and even state politicians.

#9026. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1530 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • It has been revealed that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • According to recent reports, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no intends for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

It has been revealed that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

According to recent reports, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no intends for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

Sources indicate that on the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

It has been revealed that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

It has been revealed that linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden mentioned, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden remarked. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Sources indicate that assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Industry observers note that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

In a recent development, pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden remarked, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Recent findings suggest that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden mentioned. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

Industry observers note that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden stated. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

#9025. Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights).
  • According to recent reports, ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest.
  • Sources indicate that mostafavi never fulfilled his promise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights).

According to recent reports, ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”.

Sources indicate that mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

Dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”.

Industry observers note that born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

In a recent development, mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

It has been revealed that in 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

Sources indicate that mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

Industry observers note that on his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’.

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, issues arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

In an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”.

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

In a recent development, mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary revealed that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”.

In a recent development, that evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani stated.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she mentioned.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

In a recent development, maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Sources indicate that social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Recent findings suggest that tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

According to recent reports, mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

On October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

#9022. Is an AI Data Center Coming for Your Favorite Trail? Check This Map and See

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (876 w)

Is an AI Data Center Coming for Your Favorite Trail? Check This Map and See

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.
  • It has been revealed that will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers.
  • Sources indicate that “The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks).

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

It has been revealed that will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

Sources indicate that “The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”.

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”.

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

Recent findings suggest that “The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz stated. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”.

Industry observers note that to use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site demonstrates the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz noted.

Industry observers note that the map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a tech giant called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Presently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Sources indicate that located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where significant tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”.

Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

It has been revealed that this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Sources indicate that jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

Recent findings suggest that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

Recent findings suggest that I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a substantial thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

Recent findings suggest that no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

Sources indicate that I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

Sources indicate that and so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite promptly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.
