Follow This ‘Map of Quietude’ to the Most Silent Trails in Sweden

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell).
  • It has been revealed that the invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden.
  • In a recent development, outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health issues: noise pollution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell).

It has been revealed that the invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden. “The only condition? You have to stay quiet.” Surrounded by apple orchards, with the sea just out the door, this idyllic place would be available to a few lucky travelers—as long as we maintained an air of “quietude” during our respective stays.

In a recent development, outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health issues: noise pollution. According to the European Commission, prolonged exposure to loud, chronic noise is the second largest cause of health problems contributing to cardiovascular disease, sleep disturbances, and stress-related health concerns. Spending time in naturally quiet environments can help relieve those symptoms.

Industry observers note that skåne is a region renowned for its restorative pastoral and seaside landscapes, unique rural culture, farm-to-table restaurants, and heritage traditions. Within it, The Map of Quietude—a list of 26 places mapped by a professional sound engineer—leads to many spots along Skåne’s 1,000+ miles of hiking trails. Each spot’s silence has been measured to ensure distinctly healing experiences.

I found that pausing in them to take in the stillness and beauty added something beyond a typical travel or hiking experience. It gave me insight into the true frequency of a place and what it offers: peace, an immersion in rejuvenating slowness, and awe. After my days in silence on the coast, I’ve rounded up some best trails where you can easily experience these locations of quietude, while also taking in interesting communities, historic sites, and some of Scandinavia’s most beautiful wildernesses. Sweden’s nature-centric way of life includes the right of public access, or allemansrätten, which allows hiking or camping almost anywhere in the countryside with the expectation that you will respect the land.

Distance: 7.5 miles Part of the Öresund Way, this loop is worth a detour from inland Skåne to discover a car-free island where people come to bike and hike. You can also get some of the region’s best cardamom buns at Hven Durum, a family-run bakery and mill.

Industry observers note that A quick ferry will bring you to this tiny slip of seaside heaven. Walk along the coastline and through a species-rich nature reserve for sweeping views of the Öre Sound and Copenhagen skyline. Ven’s southern headland, södra udde, is a nature reserve and designated place of quietude. See an active, mid-20th-century lighthouse nearby. Or, check out the site of 16th-century Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe’s observatory.

Distance: 7.4 Miles (bonus summit extends to 11.4 miles).

It has been revealed that starting at the edge of the Kulla peninsula in northwest Skåne, you’ll trace roughly seven and a half miles of mostly flat shoreline south from the small fishing village Mölle. One of Sweden’s first seaside resorts at the turn of the 19th century, city dwellers came here for their nature fix. Back then, Mölle was steeped in scandal when, after long hikes, men and women began swimming together in the sea nearby, something that was unthinkable at the time.

It has been revealed that the route explores nature reserves and gnarled pine forests and winds past beaches and historic towns. You’ll even pass remains of Kulla fälad, a vast historic pasture that served as a shared grazing land for livestock for centuries. In some places, ancient drystone walls are still visible. You’ll end in Höganäs, a globally renowned center of stoneware and ceramics production. It’s also a great place to explore a burgeoning creative community. Stop by The Hub Höganäs to experience local life, where artists sell heritage-steeped crafts, and locals gather for events. If you’re looking for a great place to eat, try Hubben, a local spot run by friendly Swedes.

To visit a place of Quietude, start in the spectacular Kullaberg Nature Reserve. From there, head to Håkull, the region’s highest peak. The summit offers panoramic views of the sea and Danish coastline. It will add about four miles to your trek.

In a recent development, distance: 117 miles For over 100 miles, the Österlen Way traverses the southeast corner of Skåne. This is Sweden’s famed culinary region. It’s also where my Stay Quiet Cabin was located. Starting in the medieval town of Ystad, the Österlen Way follows the Baltic Sea coast. It passes through nature reserves, national parks, and fishing villages, with inland stretches through ancient forest.

Sources indicate that among other fascinating stops, you’ll pass the hilltop stone circle, Ales Stenar. This is often referred to as “Sweden’s Stonehenge” for its similarly mysterious origins. The trail has two spots of Quietude. The first is Meditationsplatsen, a circular enclosure where people come to meditate. There’s also Gislövshammar Quarry, a 19th-century limestone quarry on the coast of its namesake fishing village. This area is known for its many orchards, farms, and excellent independent shops and bakeries.

Industry observers note that distance: 113 miles This breathtaking route hugs the wave-swept coastline of the Öresund Strait. From north to south, it passes through historic fishing villages and dramatic landscapes. It combines previously mentioned trails and quiet spots (Håkull, Mölle to Höganäs, and Ven Island) with two additional places of Quietude. There are the historic open-air cold bathing houses Pålsjöbaden and Hilleshögs dalar valley.

Hikers pass beaches, meadows, dunes and cliffs, and enter pine forests. The trail varies in difficulty before finishing with a loop around the Falsterbonäset Peninsula. Stone Age graves, medieval castle ruins, and views of the Danish coast keep things interesting. The final legs of the trail provide ample opportunities for birdwatching. It enters nature reserves that are internationally renowned habitats for many of Northern Europe’s migratory birds.

Recent findings suggest that distance: 994 miles At just under 1,000 miles (1,600 km), the region’s Skåneleden trail is a long-distance route that traverses a vast amount of the countryside’s changeable terrain. You’ll encounter rocky coast, verdant forest, national parks, and nature reserves. There are also historic sites like castles and stone circles.

According to recent reports, the Skåneleden Trail is divided into seven sub-trails by geographic area. There are 148 sections (encompassing all the previously mentioned routes). Many individual sections make for great day hikes. Or, combine them for longer treks over multiple days or weeks. Several sections are near train or bus stations, making transportation easy. Basic campsites with wind shelters and bathrooms are available along the way for those seeking a longer adventure.

**You can hear 60-minute field recordings of birdsong, waves, and wind from each of the places of quietude mentioned above on Visit Skåne’s website or Spotify.

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

Industry observers note that the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Recent findings suggest that fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#8998. Why Your Body Is Begging You to Run More Trails Instead of Roads

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1159 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Why Your Body Is Begging You to Run More Trails Instead of Roads

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Running a marathon beats up your body.
  • Maybe not, according to a new study in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise led by Mélanie Metra and Guillaume Millet of France’s Université Jean Monnet Saint-Étienne.
  • This time, Millet and his colleagues explore the question of whether road or trail running beats you up more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Cavan Images / Brent Doscher / Getty).

Running a marathon beats up your body. Your leg muscles will be damaged on a cellular level, which will translate into soreness and loss of strength that will persist for a week or more. Now imagine how much worse it would be if you were running one of those crazy mountain marathons with rough terrain and steep climbs and descents. It would be awful… right?

Maybe not, according to a new study in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise led by Mélanie Metra and Guillaume Millet of France’s Université Jean Monnet Saint-Étienne. Millet, who once finished third at the absurdly difficult 200-mile Tor des Géants mountain ultra, is one of the world’s leading trail running researchers. I’ve previously covered his research on the differences between trail and road runners, how to run uphill, how to succeed at Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, and other trail-centric topics.

This time, Millet and his colleagues explore the question of whether road or trail running beats you up more. It’s not a perfect study (for reasons we’ll come back to), but it has some very interesting—and somewhat surprising—insights.

The researchers asked runners to undertake one of the following three challenges: a simulated road marathon of roughly 26 miles on a treadmill; a simulated trail marathon on a treadmill; or an actual trail marathon on a trail outside the lab.

It has been revealed that they took a whole bunch of measures of “neuromuscular fatigue” before and after the marathon, then again one day, two days, and seven days later. These involved various measures of leg strength, maximal jumps, questionnaires about subjective pain, and blood tests to assess markers of muscle damage. The objective was to determine whether the fatigue and recovery profile would differ after the various types of running.

To make the three challenges roughly equivalent, they used the following rule of thumb: every 100 meters of uphill climbing is equivalent to an extra kilometer of flat running. With that in mind, the two trail marathons involved a total distance of 28K (just over 17 miles) with 1,400 meters (4,600 feet) of vertical ascent and descent, for a total “equivalent effort” of roughly 42K, which is the standard (flat) marathon distance.

It has been revealed that they recruited a total of 46 runners, of whom 16 were primarily road runners and were assigned to the simulated road marathon. The rest were primarily trail runners, and they were divided equally between the two trail marathon groups. The fitness, age, and training characteristics of the three groups were fairly well matched. Everyone was instructed to run the marathon as fast as possible.

The overall finding was that the road marathon beat the runners up far more than either of the two trail marathons.

It has been revealed that here, for example, is what the loss of knee extensor (i.e. quadriceps) strength looked like in the post-marathon period, with the road group in red, the treadmill trail group in light blue, and the outdoor trail group in green:.

In a recent development, the road marathoners lost more strength, and were still showing a deficit two days later. There’s a similar pattern, albeit less pronounced, in the subjective ratings of soreness and pain. (Calf muscles, on the other hand, didn’t show much difference between the groups.).

It has been revealed that the blood tests also demonstrated a major difference in muscle damage. Here are the results for one of the standard proxies of muscle damage, creatine kinase:.

The simplest interpretation is that road running causes more muscle damage than trail running.

This could be because road running is more repetitive: every stride is the same, so the same muscle fibers are being activated over and over until they get damaged. Trail running has more variety, both in the “technicity” of the terrain and in the shifts between flats, uphills, and downhills. The lack of differences between the simulated and real trail groups in the upcoming study implies that technicity doesn’t really matter (since the treadmill has a very regular surface while the outdoor trail has an irregular one), so it’s the uphills and downhills that matter.

Another possibility is that it’s not just the variability in muscle activation—it’s also that all those hills force you to slow down, and in some cases even walk, so the slower pace reduces the load on your muscles.

In a recent development, both of these factors may help explain one of the significant riddles in the results, which is why all the downhills in the trail runs didn’t cause more damage. After all, marathoners complain that the slight downhills in the opening miles of Boston wreak havoc on their legs. But Boston’s smooth and gradual descent lets runners lock into a fast (and damaging) pace, while the irregular ups and downs of the trail marathon lead to a slower pace and more variable stride.

In a recent development, there are also some possible explanations that have less to do with the inherent differences between road and trail and more to do with the study design. One is that the groups weren’t random: the road runners had trained primarily on roads, and the trail runners primarily on trails. Perhaps it’s training on trails that makes your legs more resistant to muscle damage, rather than racing on trails being less damaging. Or perhaps there are other general differences between people who choose road versus trail running. The only way to check that possibility would be to randomize people to different groups.

Recent findings suggest that the more serious problem, in my view, is that the overall average completion time for the road marathon was 3:54, compared to just 3:02 in the simulated trail group and 2:59 in the outdoor trail group. This suggests that “100 meters of climbing is equivalent to an extra kilometer of flat running” is an overly generous conversion factor. It seems very likely to me that I’d be more sore after a four-hour run than after a three-hour run, regardless of what the terrain was like.

To be fair, it’s not automatically true that longer runs cause more soreness than shorter ones. Pace matters, too. Millet himself has previously found that leg muscles are less fatigued after 200 miles at the Tor des Géants than after shorter races, because you simply can’t sustain a hard-enough-to-be-damaging pace for that long. But the difference in durations between the trail and road groups raises questions about the conclusions.

One reason I’m tempted (for better or worse) to wave away those questions is that the results fit with my own intuitions and experiences. I’ve never been as sore as I was after a road marathon; I’ve often been pleasantly surprised at how swiftly my legs bounce back after a long ramble in the forest or mountains. We can’t yet call it a scientifically proven fact, but call it a strong hunch.

Continental Divide Trail Southern Terminus Monument to Be Relocated Due to Border Wall

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T.
  • Hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) states.
  • According to recent reports, the southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T. FALLON / Contributor via Getty).

Hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) states. But with the official end of the route now trapped between two sections of steel barrier, the obelisk that marks the terminus will need to be moved.

According to recent reports, the southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall. Since 2025, that stretch has fallen inside the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area, created when the Trump administration transferred 110,000 acres administered by the Bureau of Land Management to military control.

On Friday, the CDTC said it had received confirmation that hikers would once again be able to access the terminus. As before the closure, anyone entering the NDA needs to apply online for a permit from Fort Huachuca and undergo a background check; additionally, hikers who aren’t U.S. citizens need to be chaperoned by a permitted hiker who is.

Sources indicate that “This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the CDTC said in a statement. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, the construction has created a new glitch: The Crazy Cook monument—the stone obelisk that marks the official end of the Continental Divide—is now sandwiched between the two steel barriers that make up the under-construction border wall. In an email, Audra Labert, the CDTC’s director of communications, said that while the organization had received reports that hikers had still been able to reach the monument by passing through the construction area, that arrangement is likely temporary.

“Authorities are now confirming looks to move the obelisk outside of the barrier walls for hikers to access, and passages between the barriers will eventually close,” Labert wrote. While it’s not clear when that could happen, the CDTC warned that the government would likely close the terminus to hikers again while it relocated the monument.

Construction on the border wall has complicated thru-hikers’ ability to access the southern termini of several long trails over the past year. In addition to the CDT, the federal government permanently closed access to the Arizona Trail’s southern terminus last November, a move that Matthew Nelson, the executive director of the Arizona Trail Association told Backpacker was “nothing less than a desecration.” In addition, authorities briefly banned Pacific Crest Trail hikers from touching the border wall this spring before abruptly reversing course. The under-construction barrier continues to figure in access and conservation fights along the southern border, with the Supreme Court recently ruling that the administration could continue construction of a upcoming stretch of wall in Big Bend National Park.

Recent findings suggest that one of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. Breaking: I Took a Mystery “Decision Detox” Trip With Zero Planning. Here’s What Happened.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the treehouse-like deck outside my hotel room, I took in the lush cluster of live oak and eucalyptus trees all around me, the whisper of wind and chirp of unknown birds, and the small sliver of Pacific Ocean peeking through the foliage-lined horizon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the treehouse-like deck outside my hotel room, I took in the lush cluster of live oak and eucalyptus trees all around me, the whisper of wind and chirp of unknown birds, and the small sliver of Pacific Ocean peeking through the foliage-lined horizon. I was completely at peace. The best part: I hadn’t made a single decision for the entire weekend. In fact, until just a couple days prior—the day of my trip departure—I had absolutely no idea where I’d be on this gorgeous Sunday morning.

Industry observers note that the morning of my trip, I tore open a sealed envelope that held all the information about the hotel where I’d be staying (Chaminade Resort and Spa), my itinerary (forest therapy, spa treatments, dining at The View and Lago di Como), and even the destination itself (Santa Cruz, California). This was all part of the “mystery travel” experience I eagerly agreed to, facilitated by Benchmark Resorts & Hotels and Pack Up + Go, an agency that prepares completely curated surprise vacations. Here was the deal: I filled out a survey about my preferences (my priorities while traveling, the types of hotels I liked) along with budget, then they planned the entire trip, and I wouldn’t find out details (beyond some notes about weather and packing suggestions) until I opened my envelope the morning of my departure.

As an avid traveler, eldest daughter, and strategic planner (particularly in the context of trips), I thought this format might stress me out—but I found there was a sense of freedom and lightness in not pouring into pre-trip research or curating my own itinerary. All I had to do was show up. This brand of mental surrender actually speaks to a rising travel trend: “decision detox.”.

According to recent reports, modern life can often feel like an endless series of choices. Between social media, the internet, and now AI, “we are inundated with information and access to it,” states Morgan Cutlip, PhD, psychology educator, author, and researcher. “This sends us regularly searching for the ‘right’ way of doing things rather than trusting our instincts or talking to a friend and doing what they do.”.

Industry observers note that and that absolutely applies to trip planning. “When there are so many options for something like a vacation, the more information you consume and the more reviews you read, the more uncertain you can become about your decision,” she says. “Searching out accommodations, looking up flight options, thinking through food—it becomes a ton of micro decisions packed into this one major thing that feels like it’s supposed to be extra magical, extra fun, and low stress, so the stakes feel high.”.

In a recent development, in fact, while vacations are meant to be a time to unwind and enjoy life, a 2025 survey of 1,500 Americans from YouGov found 70 percent of U.S. vacationers find their booking experience to be stress-inducing. That’s where “decision detox” trips come in, where you completely relinquish control of trip planning. The intention here is for travelers to take a break from the mental overload of everyday life and never-ending choices, in order to take a true vacation.

It has been revealed that this travel trend is on the rise. A research report published by Lemongrass, a certified B-Corp marketing agency, found a clear shift in traveler preferences for curated, all-inclusive itineraries that remove planning fatigue; a desire to visit quieter, less-crowded destinations; and a pull toward peaceful relaxation over highly stimulating experiences.

It has been revealed that and while traditional travel agents have long been planning accommodations and transportation, decision detox trips take that concept one step further with an emphasis on fully planned retreats and completely handled logistics. In my case, this meant a complete surprise trip and fully embracing the thrill of adventure that comes with not knowing your destination until the moment you depart.

“For some people, this might sound like handcuffs on a holiday, but for [people] burdened with making seemingly every decision in their families’ lives all the time, it’s heaven in the form of a pre-booked massage and meals that magically appear when desired,” Jools Sampson, founder and owner of Reclaim Yourself Retreats, wrote in the Lemongrass report.

Women are likely disproportionately affected by this kind of decision fatigue, as they tend to take on the lion’s share of trip planning. In fact, data from research organization Skift found that 82 percent of all travel decisions are made by women. This can be particularly draining for moms, who are constantly managing the logistics of life, states Cutlip, whose work often focuses on mental load discrepancies in relationships. “And if she’s the one planning it, she’s almost certainly coordinating with her partner too. Not being able to fully make decisions on her own, having to negotiate and talk each one through, adds yet another layer of work.”.

But no matter what role someone takes in a family structure, or what the underlying reason is for mental fatigue, leaning into decision detox travel can come with a whole slew of mental health benefits.

Recent findings suggest that “You eliminate all of the fatigue, overwhelm, and unnecessary stress that can come with planning a trip,” indicates Cutlip. “If you’re somebody who has the capacity to let go and you’re comfortable putting someone else in the driver’s seat, it frees you to focus on everything else a vacation requires: preparing to leave your home, getting work off, taking care of the pets, cleaning out the fridge, and then showing up ready to relax.”.

According to recent reports, benchmark decided to partner with Pack Up + Go after reading YouGov’s survey about traveler planning fatigue. “It’s a different way to approach a vacation,” says Evan Crawford, vice president of marketing for Benchmark Resorts & Hotels.

It also leads to travelers visiting locations they may not have otherwise thought to book—such as Woodinville, Washington, or the Columbia River Gorge, says Crawford. “Maybe you’ve never even heard of the place before, but now you can go there and get exposed to it and have this extraordinary experience.”.

And while a complete surprise vacation is one approach, it’s not the only way to try out a decision detox trip.

A reprieve from decision-making is at the heart of Duvine Cycling, which curates bike tour vacations that take guests everywhere from the vineyards of Burgundy to the Southern Lakes region of New Zealand.

Sources indicate that “Basically, all you have to do is show up on a trip. You don’t have to think about anything,” states CEO and co-founder Andy Levine. These active, planned trips inherently encourage people to unplug and make lasting connections with their fellow cyclists. “[We act as] their concierge, and we get to make these really cool things happen, all while on a bike.”.

Then there’s Selar, a sustainable polar expedition organization launching in early 2027. For anyone seeking a grand adventure—without all the intricate planning that often goes into these types of trips—Selar offers a chance to take a journey way up north with itineraries across Norway, Svalbard, and Greenland. Or take HX Expeditions, which, similar to a cruise model, offers all-inclusive voyages that cover excursions, meals, drinks, and gratuities—but unlike a classic cruise, these itineraries are led by onboard naturalists and historians, and their packages also include lectures, hands-on experiences, and expedition gear.

At Vermejo, a Ted Turner Reserve in Latest Mexico, each guest’s nature-focused itinerary is completely handled by their Reserve Ambassadors. There are more than 45 guided activities available, ranging from horseback riding through vast prairies, fly-fishing for Rio Grande cutthroat trout, or taking a UTV tour with the opportunity to spot elk, bear, and other substantial game.

Of course, numerous wellness resorts have been hopping on this trend for some time now, acknowledging that a true mental reset is intrinsically linked to less decision-making. BodyHoliday, an all-inclusive wellness resort in St. Lucia, asks guests to “give us your body for a week, and we’ll give you back your mind;” Sensei Lanai in Hawaii offers guided stays that cater to your individual health needs and goals; and at Renew Retreat at Calamigos Ranch in California, you can take part in a preset wellness retreat.

Sources indicate that there are also a number of retreats specifically designed for staying active. Take a running retreat with Run Wild, for example: these women-only trips are designed so you simply choose your pace and place of interest and select an already-set itinerary.

It has been revealed that the crux of these trips is rooted in analog experiences, which can help with the mental fatigue and technology overload we experience in everyday life. “I think people are really craving that opportunity to be in the moment, to be human,” states Crawford.

Sources indicate that surrendering complete control is never easy—but in the case of my trip to Santa Cruz, I found it wildly therapeutic. By not stressing about every detail, both before and during the trip, I was able to feel fully present with every item on my itinerary, including a hike through redwood forests, idly reading by the pool in my (pre-reserved) cabana, and savoring meals set to stunning views of the treetops and ocean beyond.

Sources indicate that because I opted for a road trip rather than air travel, the Pack Up + Go team even chose my rest stop on the way from Los Angeles (Paso Robles), along with recommendations for restaurants and shops to explore in the area. And this detailed research extended to my final destination in Santa Cruz, too: the team provided a meticulously curated list of shops, experiences, and more for me to explore during my final day in the area.

Before embarking on your own decision detox trip, take stock of whether this will feel freeing or cause you more stress. “My advice would be to reflect on whether you’re somebody who can actually let go of control,” indicates Cutlip. “If you’re going to turn it over to someone else and then micromanage the process, just do it yourself. If you can turn over control, fully embrace it and enjoy it.”.

For me, it was a practice in letting go of control and allowing outside help—something I think many of us could benefit from on occasion. And while I won’t necessarily be handing over the reins for every future trip I take, it was a beautiful opportunity to give my mind a bit of reprieve, to stop overthinking for a while, and simply take in the wonder of a beautiful place.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that one of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents.
  • This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack. (Photo: Stanislav Sablin/Getty Images).

Industry observers note that one of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag.

This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food.

The most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier mentioned than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp.

In a recent development, you can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible.

The bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle.

I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap.

Industry observers note that along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar.

While a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay.

According to recent reports, I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh.

Recent findings suggest that finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place.

It has been revealed that I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Big If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

According to recent reports, whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh new set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Ocun’s new Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

Edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

It has been revealed that the Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a new, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

It has been revealed that the Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional substantial-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

In a recent development, apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

It has been revealed that black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

According to recent reports, climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

What gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? By donating to Access Fund you become a member of the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, who tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens latest ones.

It has been revealed that the daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A view west from Mount Bond in Latest Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness.
  • Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.
  • Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A view west from Mount Bond in Latest Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness. (Photo: MikeCherim / Getty Images).

Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.

Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and currently partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain.

While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions.

Industry observers note that although they’d packed lights, food, and water, Latest Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) noted the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry.

Recent findings suggest that NHFG stated that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th.

In the wake of the incident, Fresh Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains.

Industry observers note that this incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

Tech Report: 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young.
  • As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions.
  • In a recent development, the earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

In a recent development, the earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”.

It has been revealed that kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most vital role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”.

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”.

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between massive and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Sources indicate that talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” mentioned Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

Recent findings suggest that as parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Even though the holidays can feel like a joyful time for many families, some stress often accompanies planning, preparing, and cooking a large meal for your loved ones. As the host, you want everyone to have a great time and enjoy the food you're serving, but you also don't want to spend your entire day in the kitchen cooking and cleaning up. If you're hoping to avoid the stress that's often accompanied by extended hours in the kitchen and trying to set a perfect table, we've put together a collection of some kitchen essentials that are going to make cooking and hosting this year feel a heck of a lot easier.

Sources indicate that every item on this list is designed to lessen your time in the kitchen and bring some of that magic back to your holiday meal. There's everything from a triple slow cooker that's not only great for cooking side dishes, but also serving them and keeping everything hot. There's also a premium electric knife that's going to make cutting up your turkey or ham a breeze. For those who appreciate convenience, there's also a buffet caddy that comes in handy when you're opting for a buffet-style meal, and you need a place to stack your plates and cutlery. Plus, there's also something special for the kids on this list that's going to help them get through the meal without a ton of fuss!

Designed to cook and serve three of your most talked-about holiday dishes, the Elite Gourmet Maxi-Matic Triple Slow Cooker Buffet is constructed with three removable ceramic 2.5-quart pots with tempered glass lids and individual cooking controls to make cooking and serving anything from stuffing to green bean casserole to roasted potatoes a breeze.

Perfect for keeping your Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner table fully stocked with cold water or juice, the Netany 4-Pack of Glass Carafe With Lids comes with four 1-liter BPA-free thickened glass serving bottles with narrow necks for easy gripping and wooden tags to label your drinks.

Comes with a compact storage case.

For perfectly done meat every time, the Meater Plus Wireless Smart Meat Thermometer is a slim stainless steel device with a dual-sensor system that can connect through Bluetooth and allows you to monitor cooking temperatures via the free app.

Industry observers note that great for accommodating a group of 8 to 12 people, the Smirly Large Bamboo Charcuterie Board is designed to impress your guests as it's a 15-by-13-inch square charcuterie board with two additional pull-out serving sections and a small drawer that contains cheese knives. You also get a round sectioned bamboo fruit tray, four small ceramic bowls that are great for dips and olives, and two slate labels.

An all-in-one service station that makes serving a festive meal for a crowd super seamless, the Sorbus Black Buffet Caddy makes a stylish and portable choice for entertaining. It's made from durable black polished steel and features two center stands for dinner, appetizer, and dessert plates, as well as four flatware compartments and a top napkin basket.

Able to be stylishly dressed up with anything from a holiday centerpiece to a vase of beautiful flowers, the Qianquhui Embroidered Dining Room Tablecloth makes a great choice for serving holiday meals for a group, as it's effortlessly elegant, waterproof, wrinkle-free, and features beautiful embroidered details and tassels.

A handy helper you can put out on the kitchen counter or table to keep your favorite dishes warm and ready to serve, the Lnniw White Electric Food Warming Mat is a large roll-out heating surface with different temperature levels and a timing function with six preset timer modes.

To help protect your table and keep the kids occupied and happy throughout your holiday meal, Tiny Expressions Christmas 12-Pack of Coloring Placemats includes 12 rectangular paper activity placemats for kids with several festive illustrations to color in, a word scramble, a tree to decorate, and more.

Sources indicate that the best part of the massive holiday feasts is usually the gravy for so many people, and the Nucookery Large Porcelain Gravy Boat With A Warmer can help keep your guests happy and eating throughout the entire meal. This 20-ounce porcelain gravy boat is meticulously designed to have a large lip to avoid spills. It also comes with a warming stand that you put a small votive candle in to keep the gravy warm and delicious.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • It has been revealed that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by Upcoming Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

It has been revealed that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Newly introduced Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Industry observers note that once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

It has been revealed that then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • In a recent development, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

Industry observers note that as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

In a recent development, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential concerns.

Recent findings suggest that honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

'You're Setting Them Up For Disappointment': People With Kids Are Sharing The Modern Parenting Trends They 100% Disagree With

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maybe you have kids of your own, maybe you’re thinking about having them somewhere down the line, or perhaps you’re pretty set on never having kids.
  • “I can’t stand how people put so much pressure on kids to play sports.
  • “Parents not watching their own behavior when it comes to screen time, frustration tolerance, discipline, etc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maybe you have kids of your own, maybe you’re thinking about having them somewhere down the line, or perhaps you’re pretty set on never having kids. In any case, you’re probably well aware that there are a whole lot of parenting trends and philosophies around raising children, and like all things parenting, people have some strong opinions. So Redditor u/The_WhiteMantis asked, “What parenting ‘trend’ do you disagree with?” Here’s what people said.

1. “I can’t stand how people put so much pressure on kids to play sports. Exposing your kid to sports is one thing; if they enjoy it, you let them keep doing it. It is completely different when you see kids in elementary school playing in every league they can be enrolled in and even doing training camps. Sure, it’s great if they are really good and you give them the tools to excel, but if your kid is mediocre at best, you are setting them up for disappointment.”.

2. “Parents not watching their own behavior when it comes to screen time, frustration tolerance, discipline, etc. You’ve got to dig deep and figure out how to model the behaviors you want your kids to do. If you are on your phone 24/7 and throw a fit every time the slightest thing inconveniences you, your kids will pick up these same behaviors.”.

3. “Breaking the bank for your kid’s birthday party by spending on expensive dessert tables, decorations, balloon backdrops, etc. Whatever happened to a simple barbecue, balloons, and a grocery store cake? People go way overboard on parties now, and it feels like it’s some way to show off on social media.”.

4. “The trend of oversharing kids’ lives on social media. It’s like turning your kid’s childhood into a reality TV show.”.

According to recent reports, 5. “Shaming other moms for how they choose to feed their kids.”.

6. “Not apologizing when you slip. Sometimes I don’t respond in the best way to my kids (at home or in my classroom) or set the best example. When that happens, I own up to it, apologize, and work to do better.”.

Industry observers note that 7. “Making your child’s entire identity revolve around their extracurricular activities. Let them be kids, not robotic machines for your bragging rights.”.

8. “Never saying ‘no’ to your child. A big part of parenting is purely getting your kids to do crucial things, whether they like them or not.”.

9. “The sad beige mom trend. If you want to make the rest of your home beige, that’s up to you. But please let your child’s nursery have some color for their development and well-being.”.

Recent findings suggest that 10. “The amount of surveillance and tracking apps that more and more parents use on their kids. It gets really sad when these kids hit college, and they are looking for ways to detach from their parents who know what and where they are up to 24/7.”.

It has been revealed that 11. “Not allowing children to be bored sometimes. We’re trying very hard to teach our seven- and four-year-olds that it’s OK (and even good) not to be entertained every second of the day. We finally had the strength to do a three-hour car ride with no electronics.”.

It has been revealed that 12. “Not teaching children proper manners and behavior. Please and thank you go a long way in this life.”.

13. “Soft parenting. I don’t necessarily disagree with soft parenting itself, but I think many parents who practice it don’t fully understand it. These people just end up allowing their kids to do whatever they want with little to no discipline.”.

14. “I’ve seen a small-yet-growing trend of homeschooled kids where the parents completely neglect actual education and basically let the kid do whatever they want. They don’t follow a standardized curriculum for the sake of ‘letting kids be kids.’ If your kid can barely read at 10 years old, you’re setting them up to fail as an adult.”.

Industry observers note that 15. “Letting them spend too much time on tablets. It’s crazy how many parents try to defend this. ‘What am I supposed to do? My 3-year-old screams in the restaurant, and then I get looks and judgment.’ You’re supposed to do what every parent has done prior to 2010 or so. You talk to your kids. You distract them. You comfort them. And if none of that works, you take them outside. Think about how bad too much screen time must be for a developing brain.”.

It has been revealed that 16. “Technology isn’t helping kids with conversation skills. A conversation usually goes back and forth with no phones involved.”.

Sources indicate that 17. “Pushing academics on young kids. I know that’s more of a societal expectation than a parenting trend, but it’s actually totally fine if your five-year-old isn’t reading yet. And your baby doesn’t need flash cards.”.

18. “Helicopter parenting. As a child that was sheltered, my parents would always intervene, and I became way too reliant on them. It wasn’t until my mid-20s that someone helped me realize what was happening, and I had to relearn how to live on my own. Sure, my parents did what they thought was best, but it backfired on me later in life. I’m still in the process of figuring out what it means to be independent and how to fight for myself.”.

It has been revealed that 19. “I hate when people dress up their baby girls in outfits meant for grown women. I see little girls’ outfits that are adorable and clearly meant for little girls. But no little girl should wear a body suit, ripped jeans, or a crop top and low-rise bellbottoms. It gives me the creeps.”.

20. “I’m all for gentle parenting, but never permissive parenting. There’s a substantial difference. Gentle parenting means you treat your child with respect. Permissive parenting means you don’t discipline your child ever, which makes them unable to deal with consequences in the future.”.

The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

Latest Update: 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • In a recent development, the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less vital than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy claims. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

In a recent development, the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

Industry observers note that 2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

Sources indicate that 4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up indicates, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

Sources indicate that 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

In a recent development, 6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

Industry observers note that 8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

Industry observers note that 9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

It has been revealed that 10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

According to recent reports, 12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

Industry observers note that 14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

In a recent development, 15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a upcoming way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

Industry observers note that 18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

Recent findings suggest that for activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

According to recent reports, 19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

Industry observers note that 21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!
